column2: Accounting separates the business from its owner
column3: An owner's personal grocery bill is a drawing when paid from business funds, rather than a business operating expense.
column4: An owner's personal grocery bill becomes a business expense simply because the business bank paid it.

column2: The assumption that an entity will continue operating for the foreseeable future
column3: Using normal depreciation rather than immediate liquidation values presumes continuing operations, unless evidence contradicts that presumption.
column4: Going concern means the entity is guaranteed never to become insolvent.

column2: Recognition based on earning and incurring rather than cash timing
column3: Services earned in March but collected in April belong to March revenue under accrual accounting.
column4: Revenue under accrual accounting is always recognised only when cash arrives.

column2: Recognising relevant expenses with the related reporting-period revenue
column3: A cost relating to this year's earned revenue need not wait for its cash payment to enter this year's expense.
column4: Matching requires all expenses to be postponed until cash is paid.

column2: Caution in making estimates under uncertainty
column3: Prudence does not justify deliberate understatement of assets or creation of hidden reserves.
column4: Prudence permits knowingly biasing every estimate downward to hide profits.

column2: The significance of information for users' decisions
column3: A small amount can be material because of its nature or context rather than size alone.
column4: Materiality can always be determined by one fixed rupee threshold for every entity.

column2: Initial measurement based on the transaction acquisition cost
column3: A machine's purchase cost is distinct from its resale value; subsequent measurement depends on the relevant accounting framework.
column4: Historical cost means every asset must remain permanently at original cost without depreciation.

column2: Assets equal liabilities plus owners' equity
column3: Purchasing furniture for cash changes asset composition without changing total assets at the transaction date.
column4: Purchasing furniture for cash necessarily increases both total assets and profit.

column2: Expenditure creating or improving benefits beyond the current period
column3: Cost directly attributable to making a new machine ready for use may form part of the asset's cost.
column4: Every payment for a new machine's installation must be treated as routine repair expense.

column2: Expenditure consumed in current operations
column3: Routine maintenance restoring normal operation is generally distinguished from an improvement extending useful life.
column4: Any repair payment is automatically a new fixed asset irrespective of its substance.

column2: Measurement of benefits arising from business reputation or excess earnings
column3: If average profit is Rs 80,000 and goodwill uses three years' purchase, goodwill is Rs 2,40,000.
column4: With average profit Rs 80,000 and three years' purchase, goodwill is Rs 26,667.

column2: Goodwill based on profits above normal earnings
column3: With actual profit Rs 90,000 and normal profit Rs 60,000, two years' purchase of super profit gives Rs 60,000 goodwill.
column4: The same data give Rs 1,80,000 goodwill under the super-profit method.

column2: Old profit share minus new profit share
column3: A partner moving from 3/5 to 1/2 sacrifices 1/10 of total profits.
column4: A partner moving from 3/5 to 1/2 gains 1/10 of total profits.

column2: New profit share minus old profit share
column3: On retirement, compensation for the outgoing partner's goodwill is charged to gaining partners in their gaining ratio.
column4: Goodwill compensation on retirement must always be charged in the old profit-sharing ratio.

column2: The account recording asset and liability revaluation at reconstitution
column3: An unrecorded liability recognised at admission causes a revaluation loss belonging to old partners.
column4: Recognising an unrecorded liability creates a revaluation gain for the incoming partner alone.

column2: Profits retained before a reconstitution event
column3: A pre-admission general reserve normally belongs to the old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio.
column4: The incoming partner automatically receives a share of every pre-admission general reserve.

column2: Partner capital is kept fixed while routine adjustments use current accounts
column3: Interest on drawings ordinarily affects the partner's current account under the fixed capital method.
column4: Interest on drawings must always reduce fixed capital even when a current account is maintained.

column2: The account used to determine profit or loss on dissolution
column3: A partner taking over a non-cash asset is debited in the partner's capital account and credited in realisation.
column4: A partner taking over an asset is credited in capital merely because the asset leaves the firm.

column2: A partner's separate creditor claim distinguished from capital
column3: In the statutory payment order, partner advances are repaid after outside debts and before partner capital.
column4: Partner capital is repaid before outside debts and partner advances.

column2: A rule allocating an insolvent partner's capital deficiency in qualifying circumstances
column3: Where the rule applies and no agreement overrides it, solvent partners bear deficiency in the relevant last-agreed capital ratio.
column4: Where the rule applies, deficiency must always be shared in profit ratio regardless of capital arrangements.

column2: Cancellation of shares for non-payment subject to applicable conditions
column3: Forfeiture removes the called-up capital on forfeited shares, while previously received capital is credited to forfeited shares.
column4: Forfeiture cancels only the unpaid call while leaving called-up share capital unchanged.

column2: Reissuing shares previously cancelled for non-payment
column3: Discount on reissue cannot exceed the forfeiture amount attributable to the shares reissued.
column4: Any desired reissue discount is permissible regardless of the amount forfeited on those shares.

column2: The amount received on shares above their face value
column3: Issuing a Rs 10 share for Rs 14 creates Rs 4 securities premium per share.
column4: Issuing a Rs 10 share for Rs 14 creates Rs 14 securities premium per share.

column2: Called share amounts that shareholders have not paid
column3: An unpaid amount already called is distinct from an amount not yet called.
column4: Uncalled share capital is automatically calls in arrears.

column2: The agreed consideration paid to acquire a business
column3: Under a net-assets method, agreed assets Rs 9 lakh less agreed liabilities Rs 3 lakh imply Rs 6 lakh consideration.
column4: Under the same net-assets method, consideration equals Rs 12 lakh.

column2: Reorganisation of capital and claims without liquidating the existing company
column3: Writing down overstated assets as part of capital reorganisation need not involve forming a new company.
column4: Internal reconstruction necessarily requires liquidating the old company and creating a new legal entity.

column2: Presenting a group as a single economic entity
column3: Intragroup receivables and payables are eliminated rather than added as claims against external parties.
column4: Intragroup receivables must remain as group assets against outside customers.

column2: Subsidiary equity attributable to owners outside the parent
column3: If the parent owns 80%, the remaining 20% interest is not automatically an external borrowing.
column4: Every non-controlling interest is classified as a loan liability simply because the parent does not own it.

column2: Profit on intragroup transfers still contained in group inventory
column3: Profit on inventory sold within the group but not yet sold outside must be eliminated from consolidated profit and inventory.
column4: Every intragroup sale immediately creates profit realised by the group against outsiders.

column2: Sales less variable cost
column3: Sales Rs 2 lakh and variable costs Rs 1.2 lakh produce Rs 80,000 contribution before fixed costs.
column4: The same data produce Rs 80,000 net profit regardless of fixed costs.

column2: Fixed cost divided by contribution per unit
column3: With fixed cost Rs 60,000 and contribution Rs 30 per unit, break-even output is 2,000 units.
column4: The same data give break-even output of 1,800 units.

column2: Contribution divided by sales
column3: With selling price Rs 200 and variable cost Rs 120, the P/V ratio is 40%.
column4: The same data give a P/V ratio of 60%.

column2: Actual or budgeted sales above break-even sales
column3: Sales Rs 5 lakh and break-even sales Rs 3 lakh give a 40% margin of safety relative to actual sales.
column4: The same data give a 60% margin of safety relative to actual sales.

column2: A future cost differing between decision alternatives
column3: An avoidable supervisor salary belongs in a make-or-buy comparison even if other factory overhead remains unchanged.
column4: Every allocated historical factory overhead is relevant whether or not it changes between alternatives.

column2: A past cost that cannot be changed by the current decision
column3: Money already spent on an irreversible study is excluded from comparing future alternatives.
column4: An irreversible past study cost becomes relevant merely because management dislikes wasting it.

column2: The benefit sacrificed by choosing an alternative
column3: Using scarce capacity internally has an opportunity cost when it displaces a profitable external order.
column4: Unused book depreciation is the only possible opportunity cost of scarce production capacity.

column2: Actual quantity multiplied by standard price minus actual price
column3: For 100 kg, standard price Rs 12 and actual price Rs 14, the price variance is Rs 200 adverse.
column4: The same price data give Rs 200 favourable merely because actual quantity equals 100 kg.

column2: Standard price multiplied by standard quantity minus actual quantity
column3: For standard quantity 90 kg, actual quantity 100 kg and standard price Rs 10, usage variance is Rs 100 adverse.
column4: The same usage data give Rs 100 favourable because actual output was completed.

column2: Comparing actual performance with budgets and analysing differences
column3: A flexible budget adjusts variable-cost allowances to the actual activity level before comparison.
column4: A flexible budget leaves every variable-cost allowance unchanged when output changes.

column2: Partially complete process output expressed as fully complete units
column3: 100 closing units that are 60% complete represent 60 equivalent conversion units, assuming that completion percentage refers to conversion.
column4: The same units represent 100 equivalent conversion units irrespective of completion.

column2: Assigning overhead through activities and appropriate cost drivers
column3: Setup-intensive low-volume products may absorb more setup cost than under a single volume-based driver.
column4: ABC requires allocating every activity cost solely by direct labour hours.

column2: Target selling price less desired profit to determine allowable cost
column3: A target price Rs 500 and required profit Rs 100 imply a target cost Rs 400.
column4: The same price and profit imply a target cost Rs 600.

column2: Continuous incremental cost reduction during ongoing production
column3: Small recurring production improvements illustrate Kaizen costing rather than only a one-time design-stage cost target.
column4: Kaizen costing applies exclusively before production begins and never during production.

column2: Considering costs across a product's entire life
column3: Development, operating support and disposal costs can all matter even when incurred in different periods.
column4: Product cost evaluation must exclude disposal and development costs because neither is current factory conversion cost.

column2: Coordinating supply and production to reduce inventory and waste
column3: Lower buffers increase dependence on reliable supply and do not mean that supply disruption risk disappears.
column4: Eliminating inventory automatically eliminates every production interruption risk.

column2: Current assets divided by current liabilities
column3: With a current ratio above one, paying part of current liabilities from cash raises the ratio if liabilities remain positive and no other items change.
column4: Paying part of current liabilities from cash leaves the ratio unchanged whenever the original ratio exceeds one and liabilities remain positive.

column2: Liquid current assets divided by current liabilities
column3: Excluding inventory can reveal a liquidity weakness hidden by a high current ratio.
column4: A high current ratio guarantees a high quick ratio regardless of the amount of inventory.

column2: A statement explaining changes in cash and cash equivalents
column3: Depreciation is added back under the indirect operating-cash-flow method because it reduced profit without using current cash.
column4: Adding back depreciation under the indirect method means depreciation itself generated cash receipts.

column2: Authoritative principles governing recognition, measurement and reporting
column3: Compliance requires the applicable reporting framework; IFRS and Indian standards cannot be treated as identical merely from their names.
column4: Every IFRS provision and every Indian accounting-standard provision are necessarily word-for-word identical.

column2: Information supporting an auditor's conclusions
column3: Third-party confirmation may provide stronger evidence of receivable existence than management's unsupported assertion.
column4: Management's unsupported oral assertion always provides more reliable evidence than external confirmation.

column2: Checking transactions against supporting documentation
column3: Checking a recorded payment against an invoice addresses transaction support rather than independently proving every asset valuation.
column4: Vouching one purchase invoice proves the valuation of every balance-sheet asset.

column2: Examining existence, ownership and related balance-sheet assertions
column3: Physically inspecting inventory supports existence but does not alone establish legal ownership or appropriate valuation.
column4: Physical inspection by itself conclusively proves ownership and valuation of all inventory.

column2: An opinion used for certain material issues that are not pervasive
column3: A material but non-pervasive misstatement can lead to a qualified opinion rather than automatically an adverse opinion.
column4: Every material misstatement must lead to an adverse opinion regardless of pervasiveness.

column2: An opinion outcome when sufficient evidence cannot be obtained with potentially pervasive effects
column3: A pervasive inability to obtain evidence differs from a proven pervasive misstatement.
column4: A disclaimer certifies that all financial statements are materially correct.

column2: Audits directed at cost, management, systems, energy, environment or safety objectives
column3: An energy audit examines energy use and efficiency rather than replacing the statutory financial-statement audit.
column4: An energy audit necessarily replaces every financial-statement audit obligation.

column2: Accounting approaches that seek to measure human-resource investment or value
column3: A model's valuation of employees does not automatically mean it qualifies for recognition as an asset under every reporting framework.
column4: Every human-resource valuation model automatically creates a recognised balance-sheet asset under all accounting standards.

column2: Accounting adjustments intended to reflect changing purchasing power or prices
column3: Restating for general purchasing power addresses a different issue from simply reporting historical nominal amounts.
column4: Historical nominal amounts already fully remove all effects of changing general purchasing power.

column2: Accounting for environmental costs, obligations and impacts
column3: Waste-treatment and restoration obligations can be relevant even when environmental costs are not separately labelled in the ledger.
column4: An environmental cost cannot exist unless the ledger account is literally named environmental cost.
